references.text: Jesus says that whoever receives you receives me—the same principle that receiving Jesus' envoys is to receive him himself.
Whoever receives one such little child in Jesus' name receives Jesus—again linked to representation and receiving Christ through his messengers.
Jesus says that whoever receives the one he sends, receives him, and whoever receives him, receives the one who sent him—a direct parallel to the principle in Luke 10:16.
Jesus says that whoever believes in him does not believe only in him, but in the one who sent him—the chain of representation between the Father and the Son.
Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him—rejecting the Son is to reject the Father, the same principle as rejecting Jesus is to reject the one who sent him.
Paul writes that whoever rejects this, rejects not a human being but God—the same principle that rejecting God's messengers is to reject God himself.
The Lord says to Samuel that the people have not rejected him, but the Lord himself—an Old Testament parallel to the principle that rejecting God's representative is to reject God.
Moses says that Israel's grumbling was not directed against him and Aaron, but against the Lord—rejecting God's sent ones is to reject God himself.
Jesus says that whoever receives this child in his name receives him, and whoever receives him receives the one who sent him—a close parallel in Luke's own gospel.
Whoever receives one such child in Jesus' name receives him, and whoever receives him receives the one who sent him—Mark's version of the same principle.
Israel's grumbling against Moses and Aaron was in reality grumbling against the Lord—to reject God's chosen leaders is to reject God.
Paul says that the Galatians did not despise him despite his weakness, but received him as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus himself—receiving the apostle was to receive Christ.
